title: 1NF Exercises
description: Eliminate repeating groups and atomicity violations to achieve First Normal Form

data.text: First Normal Form requires atomic values and no repeating groups. Violations appear as multiple values in one column or duplicate rows for the same entity.

data.title: 1NF red flags
items: Comma-separated phone numbers in one column
Repeating course columns: course1, course2, course3
Multiple values in a single VARCHAR cell

data.title: Denormalized table
data.content: A student table with repeating course columns violates 1NF.
data.code:
CREATE TABLE students (
  student_id INT,
  name VARCHAR(100),
  course1 VARCHAR(50),
  course2 VARCHAR(50),
  course3 VARCHAR(50)
);

data.title: Normalized alternative
data.content: Split repeating values into rows in a junction table.

items.question: Is a single VARCHAR always atomic?
items.answer: No. If it stores multiple conceptual values like a list of emails, it violates 1NF even if stored in one column.

items.question: Can JSON columns break 1NF?
items.answer: Yes, if the JSON represents multiple repeating entities. Use child tables instead.

items.question: What if my DB supports arrays?
items.answer: Even with array support, 1NF recommends atomic rows for simpler constraints and indexing.

data.title: Summary
points: Store exactly one value per column per row
Move repeating groups to child tables
Use junction tables for many-to-many atomicity
Avoid CSV columns for related data
data.takeaway: 1NF is the foundation of relational design. Atomic values simplify constraints, indexing, and queries.
